reading: もっとぶんぽう（えぬよんひっす）

points.explain: て-form + みる means 'do X and see' — trying something to find out how it is, tastes, works, or feels. It softens a suggestion nicely: 食べてみませんか (won't you try eating it?) is gentler than a flat command. It's written in hiragana here because みる is working as a grammar helper, not the literal verb 見る (to see) — don't confuse the two.
formation: Verb (て-form) + みる／みます
食べる → 食べて + みる → 食べてみる
着る → 着て + みる → 着てみる

examples.jp: この<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>、<ruby>辛<rt>から</rt></ruby>そうですね。食べてみます。
examples.en: This dish looks spicy. I'll try eating it.

examples.jp: この<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>、ちょっと<ruby>履<rt>は</rt></ruby>いてみてもいいですか。
examples.en: May I try on these shoes for a moment?

examples.jp: <ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>、<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでみたいです。
examples.en: I'd like to try living in Kyoto once.

dialogue.jp: この<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいカフェ、まだ行ったことがないんです。
dialogue.en: I haven't been to this new cafe yet.

dialogue.jp: じゃあ、<ruby>今度<rt>こんど</rt></ruby><ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に行ってみましょう。
dialogue.en: Then let's try going together sometime.

dialogue.jp: いいですね。何がおすすめか、聞いてみます。
dialogue.en: Sounds good. I'll try asking what they recommend.

points.tip: In shops, てみてもいいですか (may I try...) is one of the most useful phrases you'll produce — trying on clothes, sampling food, testing a demo device all use exactly this pattern.

quiz.q: You want to say 'I'll try calling him' — pick the best sentence.
quiz.ex: 〜てみます adds the 'try it and see' nuance that plain 電話します doesn't have.
why: 電話します is a flat statement of intent, missing the 'try it and see' nuance.
電話しています says you're currently on the phone — a different meaning (ongoing action).
電話しました is past tense — something already done, not something you're about to try.

quiz.q: Why is みる written in hiragana in 食べてみる?
choices: Because it's a grammar helper here, not the verb 'to see'
Because it follows a te-form only in casual speech
There's no reason, both are fine
quiz.ex: When みる/いる/おく etc. work as grammatical helpers after て-form, they're conventionally kept in hiragana even though kanji exist for their literal meanings.
why: 見る (the literal verb 'to see') is often written in kanji — it's specifically the grammatical-helper use that conventionally stays in hiragana.
This convention isn't about formality/casualness — it's about literal vs. grammatical-helper meaning.
There is a real, meaningful reason — it isn't free variation.

points.fn: Start suddenly, start, keep doing, finish doing
points.explain: Attach these to a verb's ます-stem to build a compound verb describing one phase of the action. 始める (start), 続ける (keep doing) and 終わる (finish) are fairly neutral. 出す carries a nuance of suddenness or unexpectedness — 雨が降り出した doesn't just mean 'it started raining', it means 'it suddenly started raining' (often catching you off guard).
formation: Verb (ます-stem) + 出す／始める／続ける／終わる
降る → 降り + 出す → 降り出す
話す → 話し + 続ける → 話し続ける

examples.jp: <ruby>空<rt>そら</rt></ruby>が<ruby>暗<rt>くら</rt></ruby>くなって、きゅうに雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>り出した。
examples.en: The sky went dark and it suddenly started raining.

examples.jp: この本を読み<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたら、<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まらなくなりました。
examples.en: Once I started reading this book, I couldn't stop.

examples.jp: <ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>を食べ<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わってから、テレビを見ます。
examples.en: I'll watch TV after I finish eating.

dialogue.jp: レポート、もう書き<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わりましたか。
dialogue.en: Have you finished writing the report yet?

dialogue.jp: いいえ、まだです。<ruby>今朝<rt>けさ</rt></ruby>から書き<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたばかりです。
dialogue.en: No, not yet. I only just started writing it this morning.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>って書き<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>けてくださいね。
dialogue.en: Keep on writing, good luck!

points.tip: 降り出す vs 降り始める both mean 'started raining', but 出す is the one you'll hear when someone is a little annoyed or surprised by the timing.

quiz.q: 「話し＿＿」to mean 'kept on talking' — fill the blank.
quiz.ex: 続ける specifically means to continue/keep doing an action.
why: 出した signals a sudden, often unexpected onset ('burst into talking') — not 'kept on'.
始めた means 'started' — a single moment, not ongoing continuation.
終わった means 'finished' — the opposite of 'kept on'.

quiz.q: Which best captures the nuance of <ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>き出した (about a baby)?
choices: Was crying for a while, calmly
quiz.ex: 出す after a verb often signals a sudden, somewhat unexpected onset — 'burst into tears' fits far better than a calm, ongoing cry.
why: A calm, gradual cry wouldn't use 出す, which signals suddenness.
終わる, not 出す, would mark finishing — 泣き出す is about the START, not the end.
出す means it DID happen (suddenly), not that it almost happened.

conjugation.label: Group 1 verb
conjugation.to: 書き<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>める／書き<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わる

conjugation.label: Group 2 verb
conjugation.to: 食べ<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>める／食べ<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わる

points.fn: Before doing X / during a window while X happens
points.explain: 〜前に attaches to the plain dictionary form — even when the whole sentence is about the past! — to mean 'before doing X': 寝る前に歯を磨きます (I brush my teeth before sleeping). 〜間に marks a window of time during which something else happens once: 母がいる間に、宿題をしました (I did my homework while my mother was around). Without に, 〜間 alone describes something continuous through the *whole* period instead of a single event inside it.
formation: Verb (dictionary form) + 前に
Verb (ている form) + 間に
寝る前に／子どもが寝ている間に

examples.jp: 出かける前に、<ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>閉<rt>し</rt></ruby>めておいてください。
examples.en: Please close the windows before you go out.

examples.jp: 雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>らない間に、買い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に行きましょう。
examples.en: Let's go shopping while it isn't raining.

examples.jp: 子どもが<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ている間に、<ruby>家事<rt>かじ</rt></ruby>をします。
examples.en: I do the housework while my child is sleeping.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>に行く前に、何をしておいたほうがいいですか。
dialogue.en: What should I do before going on the trip?

dialogue.jp: ホテルを<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>しておいたほうがいいですよ。
dialogue.en: You should book a hotel in advance.

dialogue.jp: わかりました。時間がある間に、やっておきます。
dialogue.en: Got it. I'll take care of it while I still have time.

points.tip: 〜間に is a small word that often decides whether a reading-comprehension answer is right — it always signals 'something happens once, inside this window', not 'the whole time'.

quiz.q: 「テレビを見ている＿＿、電話が<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>った。」 (While watching TV, the phone rang) — pick the correct particle.
quiz.ex: 間に marks a single event (the phone ringing) happening inside the window of watching TV.
why: 前に means 'before' — the phone didn't ring before you started watching.
うちに typically pairs with a state you should act within before it changes — 間に is the direct match for 'during this activity, X happened once'.
後で means 'afterward' — but the ringing happened DURING, not after, the TV-watching.

quiz.q: 「日本に来る＿＿、日本語を<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しました。」 (Before coming to Japan, I studied Japanese)
quiz.ex: 〜前に + dictionary form describes something done before the main event, regardless of overall tense.
why: 間に marks something happening inside a window, not a clear 'before' sequence.
たら is a conditional ('if/when'), not a 'before' time marker.
そう (appearance/hearsay) is unrelated to sequencing events in time.

points.fn: Doing two things at the same time
points.explain: Attach ながら to a verb's ます-stem to describe two actions happening at once, done by the same person. The verb right before ながら is the 'background' action; the main verb of the sentence is the primary one. 音楽を聴きながら勉強する = 'study while listening to music' — studying is the main activity, listening is what's happening alongside it.
formation: Verb (ます-stem) + ながら
聞く → 聞き + ながら → 聞きながら

examples.jp: いつも<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>き</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します。
examples.en: I always study while listening to music.

examples.jp: テレビを見ながら<ruby>晩<rt>ばん</rt></ruby>ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を食べました。
examples.en: I ate dinner while watching TV.

examples.jp: アルバイトをしながら、大学に<ruby>通<rt>かよ</rt></ruby>っています。
examples.en: I'm attending university while working a part-time job.

dialogue.jp: いつも<ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>きながらスマホを見ていますね。<ruby>危<rt>あぶ</rt></ruby>ないですよ。
dialogue.en: You're always looking at your phone while walking. That's dangerous.

dialogue.jp: すみません、気をつけます。
dialogue.en: Sorry, I'll be careful.

points.tip: 食べながら話す (talking while eating) is a very natural phrase to describe casual meals with friends — a nice one to have ready for small talk about your day.

quiz.q: 「コーヒーを飲み＿＿、<ruby>新聞<rt>しんぶん</rt></ruby>を読みます。」
quiz.ex: ながら links two simultaneous actions by the same person — drinking coffee while reading the newspaper.
why: まえに means 'before' — but the two actions here happen at the same time, not in sequence.
あとで means 'after' — same issue, wrong relationship between the two actions.
そうに is an adverbial form of appearance-そう, unrelated to simultaneous actions.

quiz.q: In <ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>き</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する, which is the main activity?
choices: Both equally, with no main one
quiz.ex: The verb after ながら (勉強する) is the main action; 聴きながら describes what's happening alongside it.
why: Listening is the backgrounded action (marked by ながら), not the main one.
ながら specifically marks one action as secondary/backgrounded — they aren't treated equally.
It's not just 'background info' — listening is a real simultaneous action, just the secondary one.

points.explain: The volitional form (行こう, 食べよう, しよう, 来よう) is the plain/casual version of 〜ましょう — used to suggest something to a close friend, or to think out loud to yourself ('I guess I'll...'). 〜つもりです expresses a settled personal intention — stronger and more decided than 〜たいです (just a wish), and more personal than 予定です (a schedule, which can be set by other people or circumstances).
formation: Godan: う→おう (行く→行こう)
Ichidan: る→よう (食べる→食べよう)
する→しよう／来る→来よう
Verb (dictionary form) + つもりです

examples.jp: そろそろ<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ろう。
examples.en: Let's head home soon. / I think I'll head home.

examples.jp: 来年、日本で<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>くつもりです。
examples.en: I intend to work in Japan next year.

examples.jp: もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えてから<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めようと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。
examples.en: I think I'll decide after thinking a bit more.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>夏休<rt>なつやす</rt></ruby>み、どうするつもりですか。
dialogue.en: What do you intend to do for summer break?

dialogue.jp: <ruby>沖縄<rt>おきなわ</rt></ruby>に行こうと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています。
dialogue.en: I'm thinking of going to Okinawa.

dialogue.jp: いいですね！わたしも<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に行こうかな。
dialogue.en: Nice! Maybe I'll come along too.

points.tip: 〜（よ）うと思っています ('I'm thinking of doing...') softens an intention nicely — more tentative than つもり, and very natural in everyday conversation about future plans.

quiz.q: Casual equivalent of 食べましょう:
quiz.ex: 食べよう is the plain/volitional form, matching casual 食べましょう.
why: 食べている is progressive ('is eating') — unrelated to 'let's eat'.
食べれば is conditional ('if [we] eat') — a different meaning.
食べさせる is causative ('make/let [someone] eat') — a different meaning.

quiz.q: Which sounds like the most firmly decided plan?
choices: 日本に行く<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>です
日本に行くつもりです
quiz.ex: つもりです expresses a settled personal intention — stronger than たい (wish) and more personally-decided than 予定 (a schedule).
why: たいです is just a wish/desire — the least firm of the four.
予定です describes a scheduled plan, which can be set by circumstances rather than firm personal resolve.
行こうかな ('maybe I'll go') is tentative, thinking-out-loud — the least decided, not the most.

conjugation.label: 〜つもり (plain form)
conjugation.to: 書くつもり／書かないつもり

points.jp: 〜たほうがいいです／〜ないほうがいいです
points.romaji: ~ta hou ga ii desu / ~nai hou ga ii desu
points.explain: This is how you give advice or a recommendation in Japanese — literally 'the side of having done X is good'. For positive advice, use the plain PAST form even though you're talking about something not done yet (行ったほうがいいです, not 行くほうがいい — the past form is the fixed pattern here). For negative advice, use the plain negative non-past form (行かないほうがいいです). It can sound a little direct/strong, so softening with と思います or です/だ removed in casual speech is common among friends.
formation: Verb (た-form) + ほうがいいです
Verb (ない-form) + ほうがいいです
病院に行ったほうがいいです／お酒を飲まないほうがいいです

examples.jp: <ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>があるなら、<ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>に行ったほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: If you have a fever, you'd better go to the hospital.

examples.jp: <ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>、あまり<ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>いものを食べないほうがいいです。
examples.en: You'd better not eat sweet things much at night.

examples.jp: <ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby>な<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>ですから、コピーを<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>っておいたほうがいいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。
examples.en: Since it's an important document, I think you'd better make a copy.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>頭<rt>あたま</rt></ruby>が<ruby>痛<rt>いた</rt></ruby>いんです。
dialogue.en: I have a headache.

dialogue.jp: それなら、<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く休んだほうがいいですよ。
dialogue.en: In that case, you'd better rest soon.

dialogue.jp: そうですね。今日は<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>しないほうがいいですね。
dialogue.en: You're right — I'd better not push myself today.

points.tip: Doctors, hotel staff and coworkers all use this pattern constantly — recognizing the た-form + ほうがいい shape instantly will save you from over-parsing sentences that are just friendly advice.

quiz.q: 'You'd better not go out today' (it's raining hard) — pick the correct form.
choices: 出かけるほうがいいです
出かけたほうがいいです
出かけないほうがいいです
quiz.ex: Negative advice uses the plain negative (ない) form + ほうがいいです.
why: This is positive advice TO go out — the opposite of what's needed.
Also positive advice to go out (just using the fixed た-form pattern) — still the wrong direction.
てもいい grants permission to go out — doesn't express advice against it.

quiz.q: Why is 行ったほうがいい (past-form) used for advice about the future?
choices: It's a mistake commonly made by natives
ほうがいい is a fixed pattern that takes the た-form for positive advice
It means the advice is about something already done
quiz.ex: た-form + ほうがいい is simply the fixed grammatical shape for positive advice, regardless of when the advised action happens.
why: It's not a mistake — it's the standard, correct grammatical shape.
The advice is about a future action; the た-form here doesn't mean the action already happened.
Politeness is handled separately (です/ます) — the た-form's role here is purely grammatical.

points.explain: Attaching か to a question word makes it indefinite — 何か (something), だれか (someone), どこか (somewhere), いつか (sometime) — used when you don't know or don't need to specify what/who/where. Attaching でも instead makes it all-inclusive — 何でも (anything at all), だれでも (anyone), どこでも (anywhere), いつでも (anytime) — often used to make an offer sound completely open, or to say there's no restriction at all.
formation: 疑問詞 + か（不特定 — some-）
疑問詞 + でも（全部 — any- at all）
何か食べますか／何でも食べられます

examples.jp: 何か飲み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>はいかがですか。
examples.en: Would you like something to drink?

examples.jp: アレルギーはないので、何でも食べられます。
examples.en: I don't have allergies, so I can eat anything at all.

examples.jp: <ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>があれば、いつでも聞いてください。
examples.en: If you have questions, feel free to ask anytime.

dialogue.jp: どこか行きたいところはありますか。
dialogue.en: Is there somewhere you'd like to go?

dialogue.jp: どこでもいいですよ、<ruby>任<rt>まか</rt></ruby>せます。
dialogue.en: Anywhere's fine, I'll leave it up to you.

points.tip: だれでもいいです (anyone's fine) and どこでもいいです (anywhere's fine) are extremely handy, natural-sounding ways to defer a decision to whoever you're with — much more common than picking something specific.

quiz.q: 「＿＿<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれませんか。」 (Could someone help me?) — fill the blank.
quiz.ex: だれか = 'someone' (unspecified) — perfect for a general request for help.
why: だれでも means 'anyone at all' — too broad/insistent for a simple general request.
だれが would ask 'who [specifically]' — expecting a named answer, not making a request.
だれに would mean 'to whom' — doesn't fit this sentence structure.

quiz.q: 「この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>は＿＿入れます。」 meaning 'anyone can enter this shop' —
quiz.ex: だれでも = 'anyone at all', matching the all-inclusive meaning.
why: だれか means 'someone [unspecified]' — narrower than the all-inclusive meaning needed.
だれと means 'with whom' — unrelated to who may enter.
だれの means 'whose' — unrelated to permission to enter.

points.explain: は marks what the sentence is ABOUT — the topic, usually something already known or being set up for comment, and often implies a soft contrast ('as for X...'). が marks the grammatical SUBJECT, frequently introducing brand-new information or directly answering a who/what question. 私は学生です answers 'what about you?'; だれが来ましたか／田中さんが来ました uses が because the answer is new, focused information. This distinction quietly causes more subtly-off sentences at N4 than almost any single grammar point — it's rarely tested as a fill-in-the-blank, but it shows up constantly in reading comprehension nuance.
formation: は — topic, known info, contrast (私は学生です)
が — subject, new info, answers a question-word (だれが／何が)

examples.jp: わたしは<ruby>会社員<rt>かいしゃいん</rt></ruby>です。
examples.en: As for me, I'm an office worker. (topic)

examples.jp: だれが電話をかけましたか。<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんがかけました。
examples.en: Who made the call? Tanaka-san did. (が — new/focused info)

examples.jp: この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>はラーメンが<ruby>有名<rt>ゆうめい</rt></ruby>です。
examples.en: This shop — [its] ramen is famous. (は sets the topic, が marks what's famous within it)

dialogue.jp: <ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんは今日来ますか。
dialogue.en: Is Yamada-san coming today? (は — asking about a known topic)

dialogue.jp: いいえ、<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんは来ませんが、<ruby>鈴木<rt>すずき</rt></ruby>さんが来ます。
dialogue.en: No, Yamada-san isn't coming, but Suzuki-san is. (が — contrastive new info)

points.tip: A fast rule of thumb: if you could answer the question 'who/what?' with the word, use が. If the word is what you're commenting ABOUT, use は. It won't cover every case, but it resolves most N4-level confusion.

quiz.q: 「＿＿来ましたか」 answered by 「<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが来ました」 — which particle fits the question?
quiz.ex: が pairs with question words like だれ/何 when asking for new, specific information.
why: だれは would treat 'who' as a known topic, which conflicts with が being needed to introduce new, specific information.
だれを would make 'who' the object being acted upon, not the one doing the coming.
だれの ('whose') doesn't fit this sentence structure at all.

quiz.q: Which sentence introduces Tanaka as a brand-new topic being commented on afterward?
choices: <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが来ました。
<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんは学生です。
だれが<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんですか。
quiz.ex: は sets 田中さん up as the topic, with 学生です as the comment about him — the classic は use case.
why: が here marks Tanaka as new/focused information (answering 'who came'), not as a topic being commented on.
Same issue — が marks new information here, not a topic being introduced for comment.
This is a question, not a statement introducing Tanaka as a topic.

points.fn: Change moving toward now vs. away from now
points.explain: Attached to a verb of change, てくる frames the change as unfolding up through the present moment — だんだん暖かくなってきました (it's been gradually getting warmer [and still is now]). ていく frames a change continuing on from now into the future — これからも日本語を勉強していきます (I'll keep on studying Japanese from here on). Both also keep their plain, literal meaning of physical motion toward/away from the speaker with motion verbs (歩いてくる — walk over here / 歩いていく — walk off/away).
formation: Verb (て-form) + くる — change up to now / motion toward speaker
Verb (て-form) + いく — change from now on / motion away from speaker

examples.jp: <ruby>空<rt>そら</rt></ruby>がだんだん<ruby>暗<rt>くら</rt></ruby>くなってきました。
examples.en: The sky has been gradually getting darker.

examples.jp: これから<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くなっていくでしょう。
examples.en: It'll probably keep getting colder from here on.

examples.jp: 雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ってきたので、<ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってきてください。
examples.en: It's started raining, so please bring an umbrella.

dialogue.jp: 日本語、だいぶ<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>になってきましたね。
dialogue.en: Your Japanese has really been getting better.

dialogue.jp: ありがとうございます。これからも<ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>って<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>していきます。
dialogue.en: Thank you. I'll keep working hard at studying from here on.

points.tip: なってきた vs なっていく is a small but very tellable difference in tone: きた looks back at a change that's been building up to now; いく looks forward at a change that will keep going. Native speakers use both constantly when small-talking about weather and seasons.

quiz.q: 「これから<ruby>涼<rt>すず</rt></ruby>しく＿＿でしょう。」 (It'll probably keep getting cooler from now)
quiz.ex: ていく frames a change continuing onward from the present into the future.
why: てきた frames the change as building up TO NOW, not continuing onward into the future.
そうだった (past appearance) reports a past guess, not an ongoing future trend.
らしかった (past hearsay) reports something you'd heard, not a forward-looking trend.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>暖<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かく＿＿ました。」 (It's been getting warmer lately, up to now)
quiz.ex: てきた frames the change as building up to the present moment — exactly what 'lately, up to now' describes.
why: ていく points forward from now — the sentence is about change building up TO the present, which needs てきた instead.
なるところ means 'about to become' — a point right before the change, not a gradual build-up.
なったばかり means 'just became' a moment ago — not a gradual trend over 'lately'.

conjugation.label: Group 1 verb
conjugation.to: 書いてくる／書いていく

conjugation.label: Group 2 verb
conjugation.to: 食べてくる／食べていく

points.explain: For an i-adjective, drop い and add くなる (寒い → 寒くなる, 'become cold'). For a na-adjective or noun, add になる (有名 → 有名になる, 'become famous'). This describes a change that happens on its own. Don't confuse it with する, which describes actively making something that way — 部屋をきれいにする ('to make/tidy the room clean' — someone does it) versus 部屋がきれいになる ('the room becomes clean' — it just happens/results).
formation: i-adjective (drop い) + くなる — 寒い → 寒くなる
na-adjective／noun + になる — 静か → 静かになる
contrast: 〜くする／〜にする = make it that way (deliberately)

examples.jp: 今年の冬は<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>より<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くなりました。
examples.en: This winter got colder than last winter.

examples.jp: <ruby>練習<rt>れんしゅう</rt></ruby>して、テニスが<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>になりました。
examples.en: I practiced and got good at tennis.

examples.jp: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は来月、先生になります。
examples.en: He's going to become a teacher next month.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby>、日本語のニュースが<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かるようになりました。
dialogue.en: Lately I've become able to understand Japanese news a little.

dialogue.jp: すごいですね！だんだん<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>になっていますね。
dialogue.en: That's amazing! You're gradually getting better and better.

points.tip: 〜ようになる (become ABLE to / come to do X, added to a verb rather than an adjective) is the natural extension of this pattern — 分かるようになりました, 話せるようになりました — and turns up constantly in diary-style reading passages.

quiz.q: 'The room became clean (on its own / as a result)' — pick the correct sentence.
choices: <ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>をきれいにしました
<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>がきれいになりました
<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>はきれいにします
quiz.ex: になる describes a change happening/resulting on its own, distinct from にする (someone deliberately making it that way).
why: にする + を means someone deliberately made it clean — the opposite of 'on its own'.
にします (future/habitual にする) again implies deliberate action by someone.
でした just states it WAS clean — no sense of change/becoming at all.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い→＿＿」 correct くなる form:
quiz.ex: Drop い from the i-adjective 安い and add くなる: 安くなる.
why: 安になる drops too much — you need to keep く after removing い.
安いくなる keeps the い that should be dropped before adding くなる.
安くする is 'make cheap' (deliberate action by someone), not 'become cheap' on its own.

points.fn: Emphasizing a surprisingly large amount vs. only
points.explain: A number/quantity + も (三時間も待ちました — waited a whopping three hours) frames the amount as surprisingly large. A number/quantity + しか + a NEGATIVE verb (三時間しか寝ませんでした — only slept three hours) frames it as surprisingly small — しか always needs a negative verb at the end, even though the overall meaning isn't negative in English. Mixing these up (しか with an affirmative verb, or も expecting a small amount) is a very common N4 mistake.
formation: 数量 + も + affirmative verb — emphasizes 'as many/much as'
数量 + しか + negative verb — emphasizes 'only'
三時間も／三時間しか〜ません

examples.jp: この本は1000円もしました。
examples.en: This book cost as much as 1000 yen!

examples.jp: <ruby>財布<rt>さいふ</rt></ruby>に500円しかありません。
examples.en: I only have 500 yen in my wallet.

examples.jp: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>は三時間しか<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ませんでした。
examples.en: I only slept three hours yesterday.

dialogue.jp: 今日のテスト、どうでしたか。
dialogue.en: How was today's test?

dialogue.jp: <ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しかったです。時間が10<ruby>分<rt>ぷん</rt></ruby>しかなかったので、<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わりませんでした。
dialogue.en: It was hard. There was only 10 minutes, so I didn't finish it all.

points.tip: しか sentences always end negative in Japanese even when the English translation sounds positive ('only') — this mismatch is exactly why it trips learners up in fill-in-the-blank questions.

quiz.q: 「クラスに学生が三人＿＿いません。」 (There are only three students)
quiz.ex: しか + negative verb (いません) = 'only three'. も would require an affirmative verb and would flip the nuance to 'as many as three'.
why: も + affirmative would flip the meaning to 'as many as three' — but the verb here is negative (いません), which needs しか.
でも means 'even/any' (だれでも, 'anyone') — doesn't fit a quantity statement like this.
とか is a casual listing particle ('or something like'), unrelated to quantity emphasis.

quiz.q: 'I waited as long as two hours!' — which fits?
choices: 二時間も<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちました
二時間しか<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちませんでした
二時間ぐらい<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちました
quiz.ex: 数量 + も + affirmative verb emphasizes the amount was surprisingly large.
why: しか + negative verb means 'only' — the opposite emphasis from 'as long as'.
ぐらい just means 'about/approximately' — no sense of 'surprisingly long'.
This mixes in an English word and isn't valid Japanese.

points.jp: 〜と思います／〜と言っていました
points.explain: と思います reports your own opinion or guess about a plain-form clause — 明日は雨が降ると思います (I think it'll rain tomorrow). と言っていました reports something someone else said, keeping roughly their own words — 田中さんはもう帰ると言っていました (Tanaka said he was already heading home). Both use と to mark the quoted content right before it; the verb that follows と tells you whose voice the sentence is really reporting.
formation: Plain form + と思います — your own opinion/guess
Plain form + と言っていました — someone else's reported speech
田中さんは来ると言っていました

examples.jp: この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。
examples.en: I think this problem is difficult.

examples.jp: <ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>国に<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていました。
examples.en: My friend said she was going back to her country next week.

examples.jp: <ruby>店員<rt>てんいん</rt></ruby>さんは、これが<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby>人気だと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていました。
examples.en: The shop clerk said this is the most popular.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんはパーティーに来るんですか。
dialogue.en: Is Yamada-san coming to the party?

dialogue.jp: <ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいから来られないと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていましたよ。
dialogue.en: He said he's busy so he can't come.

dialogue.jp: そうですか。<ruby>残念<rt>ざんねん</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。
dialogue.en: I see. I think that's a shame.

points.tip: In reading passages, と言っていました almost always signals the answer to a 'what did X say' comprehension question — scan for it directly rather than re-reading the whole paragraph.

quiz.q: 'I think it's going to rain tomorrow' — pick the correct sentence.
choices: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ってと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったら<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るし<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います
quiz.ex: Plain form (降る) + と思います is the correct pattern for reporting your own opinion/guess.
why: と思います needs the plain form directly before と (降ると), not the て-form (降って).
たら思います isn't a standard pattern — と is the particle that pairs with 思う here.
し思います also isn't standard — し lists reasons and doesn't combine with 思う this way.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんはもう<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る＿＿いました。」 (Tanaka said he was already heading home)
quiz.ex: と marks the quoted content right before 言う — と言っていました reports someone else's words.
why: を would mark a direct object, but the particle that introduces quoted speech content before 言う is と, not を.
が would mark who is speaking, not introduce the quoted content.
は would mark a topic, not introduce quoted content before 言う.

conjugation.label: な-adjective
conjugation.to: <ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います

conjugation.label: Noun
conjugation.to: 学生だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います

check.q: 「このシャツ、<ruby>着<rt>き</rt></ruby>＿＿もいいですか。」 (may I try it on?)
check.ex: 〜てみてもいいですか asks permission to try something out — the shop phrase you'll use most.

check.q: 「<ruby>空<rt>そら</rt></ruby>が<ruby>暗<rt>くら</rt></ruby>くなって、<ruby>急<rt>きゅう</rt></ruby>に雨が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>り＿＿。」 (suddenly started)
check.ex: 出す adds a nuance of suddenness that plain 始める doesn't carry.

check.q: 「<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る＿＿、<ruby>歯<rt>は</rt></ruby>を<ruby>磨<rt>みが</rt></ruby>きます。」
check.ex: 〜前に takes the dictionary form and means 'before doing'.

check.q: 「<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>が<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ている＿＿、<ruby>掃除<rt>そうじ</rt></ruby>をしました。」 (one event inside that window)
check.ex: 間に marks a single event happening inside a window. 間 without に would mean the whole time.

check.q: 「テレビを見＿＿、ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を食べます。」
check.ex: ます-stem + ながら links two simultaneous actions by the same person.

check.q: 「来年、<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>する＿＿です。」 (a settled intention)
check.ex: つもりです expresses a decided personal intention.

check.q: 「<ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>があるなら、<ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>へ行っ＿＿ですよ。」
check.ex: Positive advice uses the plain PAST form: 行ったほうがいいです.

check.q: 「お<ruby>酒<rt>さけ</rt></ruby>は飲ま＿＿ほうがいいですよ。」
check.ex: Negative advice uses the plain negative non-past: 飲まないほうがいい.

check.q: 「＿＿食べたいものはありますか。」 (anything in particular?)
check.ex: 何か = 'something/anything (unspecified)', the right form for an open offer.

check.q: 「アレルギーはないので、＿＿食べられます。」 (anything at all)
check.ex: 何でも is the all-inclusive form: there's no restriction at all.

check.q: 「だれ＿＿来ましたか。」「<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんです。」
check.ex: Question words like だれ/何 take が when asking for new, specific information.

check.q: 「<ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby>、日本語が<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>になっ＿＿ました。」 (a change building up to now)
check.ex: てくる frames the change as unfolding up through the present moment.

check.q: 「これからも日本語を<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>し＿＿。」 (continuing on from now)
check.ex: ていく points the change forward from now into the future.

check.q: 「<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>は3時間＿＿<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ませんでした。」 (only three hours)
check.ex: しか always pairs with a negative verb and frames the amount as surprisingly small.

reading: さらにぶんぽう（えぬよんひっす に）

points.jp: 名詞を修飾する節（関係節）
points.fn: Describing a noun with a whole clause ('the book that...')
points.explain: A whole clause can sit directly in front of a noun to describe it, using the plain (dictionary / plain-past / plain-negative) form of the verb right before the noun — no word for 'that/which/who' is needed. わたしが昨日買った本 = 'the book that I bought yesterday'. The clause always comes BEFORE the noun it modifies, the reverse of English word order. Note that が, not は, usually marks the subject inside the clause, even though は would mark it in a stand-alone sentence.
formation: Verb (plain form) + Noun
わたしが昨日買った本 → 'the book I bought yesterday'
日本語を話す人 → 'a person who speaks Japanese'

examples.jp: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が買った本はとても<ruby>面白<rt>おもしろ</rt></ruby>かったです。
examples.en: The book I bought yesterday was very interesting.

examples.jp: 日本語を話す人に<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いました。
examples.en: I met a person who speaks Japanese.

examples.jp: あそこに<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>っている人はだれですか。
examples.en: Who is that person standing over there?

dialogue.jp: この間<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>してくれた本、もう読みましたか。
dialogue.en: Have you already read the book you lent me the other day?

dialogue.jp: いいえ、まだです。今読んでいる本を先に<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わらせます。
dialogue.en: No, not yet. I'll finish the book I'm currently reading first.

dialogue.jp: わかりました、<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>がなくていいですよ。
dialogue.en: Got it, no rush.

points.tip: In reading passages, watch for a plain-form verb immediately followed by a noun — that whole clause in front is one big 'adjective', not a separate sentence. Translating strictly left-to-right trips up a lot of beginners here.

quiz.q: 「これは＿＿本です。」 (This is the book I bought yesterday)
choices: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>買った
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>買った
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>買います
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>買くて
quiz.ex: Inside a noun-modifying clause the subject is usually marked with が, not は, and the verb takes a plain form — here plain past 買った, since it's something already bought.
why: は can mark the subject of a stand-alone sentence, but が is the natural choice for the subject inside a clause modifying a noun.
Modifying clauses need the PLAIN form, not the polite ます form (買います).
買くて isn't a valid conjugation of 買う at all.

quiz.q: 「あそこで話している人は<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんです。」 means:
choices: The person talking over there is Tanaka.
Tanaka is talking to that person over there.
Tanaka asked that person to talk.
That person is waiting for Tanaka.
quiz.ex: 話している人 ('the person who is talking') modifies 人 — the whole clause describes who 田中さん is.
why: There's no separate mention of Tanaka doing the talking TO someone here — 話している人 modifies 人 itself, identifying that person as Tanaka.
Nothing in the sentence describes anyone being asked to talk.
There's no mention of waiting anywhere in this sentence.

conjugation.label: Verb ＋noun
conjugation.to: 書く人／書いた人／書かない人

points.explain: Attach かどうか to a plain-form clause to embed an unsure yes/no question inside a bigger sentence — 明日晴れるかどうかわかりません (I don't know whether it'll be sunny tomorrow or not). This differs from plain 〜か alone, which usually pairs with a question word to embed an open question (何を買うか教えてください). With na-adjectives and nouns, だ is dropped before か: 便利かどうか, not 便利だかどうか.
formation: Plain form + かどうか (+ わかりません／教えてください／確認します, etc.)
行く → 行くかどうか
na-adjective／noun: 便利 → 便利かどうか (だ is dropped)

examples.jp: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が来るかどうかまだわかりません。
examples.en: I still don't know whether he's coming or not.

examples.jp: このレストランが今日<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いているかどうか電話で聞いてみます。
examples.en: I'll call and ask whether this restaurant is open today or not.

examples.jp: その話が<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>かどうか、<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>したほうがいいです。
examples.en: You should check whether that story is true or not.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>のパーティー、<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんも来ますか。
dialogue.en: Is Yamada-san also coming to tomorrow's party?

dialogue.jp: さあ、来るかどうかわかりません。<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていましたから。
dialogue.en: Hmm, I don't know whether he's coming or not. He said he was busy.

dialogue.jp: そうですか。じゃあ、後で聞いてみます。
dialogue.en: I see. Well, I'll ask him later then.

points.tip: Watch for だ dropping before かどうか with noun/na-adjective sentences — 元気だかどうか is a common mistake; 元気かどうか is correct.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>にパーティーに来る＿＿、まだわかりません。」
quiz.ex: かどうか embeds a yes/no question ('whether or not he'll come') inside わかりません. のに/ので don't fit an embedded question at all.
why: か alone typically pairs with a question word (何か／だれか) or forms a direct question — by itself it doesn't express 'whether or not' without どう.
のに marks an unexpected contrast, not an embedded yes/no question.
ので gives a reason, unrelated to expressing uncertainty about whether something is true.

quiz.q: 「この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>＿＿、みんなに聞いてみましょう。」
quiz.ex: だ is dropped directly before かどうか with na-adjectives/nouns — 便利かどうか, not 便利だかどうか.
why: だ must be dropped directly before かどうか.
な is the attributive form used before a noun — かどうか attaches straight to the plain adjective stem without な here.
かどうかだ reverses the correct order; だ never follows かどうか like this.

points.explain: Attach ばかり to the plain PAST (た) form of a verb to say an action just finished — from the speaker's felt sense of time, not necessarily an exact minute. 今来たばかりです (I just got here). It's often used to explain why something hasn't happened yet or why a result still feels fresh: 習ったばかりなので、まだ上手じゃないです. Note ばかり behaves like a noun/na-adjective, so な appears before ので/です-based continuations: 買ったばかりなので.
formation: Verb (た-form) + ばかり(です)
来る → 来た＋ばかり → 来たばかり
before ので／な-continuations: 買ったばかりなので

examples.jp: 日本に<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたばかりです。
examples.en: I just arrived in Japan.

examples.jp: この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>習<rt>なら</rt></ruby>ったばかりで、まだよく<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えていません。
examples.en: I just learned this kanji, so I don't remember it well yet.

examples.jp: さっき<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたばかりなので、まだ<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>いです。
examples.en: I just woke up, so I'm still sleepy.

dialogue.jp: もうご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>食べましたか。
dialogue.en: Have you eaten yet?

dialogue.jp: いいえ、まだです。今<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたばかりなんです。
dialogue.en: No, not yet. I just woke up.

dialogue.jp: じゃあ、<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を食べましょう。
dialogue.en: Then let's eat breakfast together.

points.tip: たばかり describes psychological recency, not a strict time limit — 三年前に結婚したばかりです ('we just got married, three years ago') is fine if it still feels recent to the speaker. Don't over-literalize it as 'within the last few minutes'.

quiz.q: 「このパソコンは<ruby>先週<rt>せんしゅう</rt></ruby>＿＿ので、まだ<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>がよくわかりません。」
quiz.ex: たばかり requires the plain PAST (た) form, and behaves like a na-noun before ので, so な is inserted: 買ったばかりなので.
why: ばかり (just did) attaches to the PAST た-form, not the plain non-past 買う.
ばかり acts like a noun/na-adjective before ので, so な must appear between them — ばかりの is the wrong connector here.
ている describes an ongoing state, not a just-completed action — ばかり pairs with the plain past た-form instead.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>したばかりです。」 is best translated as:
choices: We've been married for a long time.
quiz.ex: たばかり marks something that (subjectively) just happened — here, a recent marriage.
why: たばかり marks something that already happened, not something upcoming.
たばかり emphasizes recency, the opposite of 'a long time'.
たばかり states a completed fact, not a possibility.

conjugation.label: Group 3 verb
conjugation.to: したばかり／来たばかり

points.fn: Showing outward signs of a feeling (about someone else)
points.explain: Words like 欲しい (want) and 〜たい (want to do) directly describe the SPEAKER's own feelings, so using them plainly for someone else (彼は水が欲しいです) sounds odd. To talk about a third person's want or feeling as something you observe from outside, drop the final い and add がる, which then behaves like a regular verb — often used as 〜がっている for an observable ongoing state: 弟は新しいゲームを欲しがっています (my little brother wants a new game — you can tell).
formation: い-adjective (drop い) + がる → 欲しい → 欲しがる
〜たい (drop い) + がる → 行きたい → 行きたがる
often used as 〜がっている for an observable ongoing state

examples.jp: <ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>欲<rt>ほ</rt></ruby>しがっています。
examples.en: My little sister wants new shoes (you can tell).

examples.jp: 子どもはお<ruby>化<rt>ば</rt></ruby>けの話を<ruby>怖<rt>こわ</rt></ruby>がります。
examples.en: Children get scared of ghost stories.

examples.jp: <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>はいつも外で<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>びたがります。
examples.en: My little brother always wants to play outside.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>さん、<ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby>どうですか。
dialogue.en: How's your son doing lately?

dialogue.jp: <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>欲<rt>ほ</rt></ruby>しがっていて、毎日それしか話さないんです。
dialogue.en: He wants a new bicycle, and that's all he talks about every day.

dialogue.jp: かわいいですね。
dialogue.en: That's cute.

points.tip: がる only describes someone else's outward, observable state — never your own feelings (keep using plain 欲しい／〜たい for yourself). Mixing this up is one of the most common N4-level mistakes.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>はアイスクリームを＿＿。」 (My little brother wants ice cream — describing his behavior, not your own feeling)
quiz.ex: For a third person's want, drop い from 欲しい and add がる (often がっている for an observable state) — 欲しがっています, not the direct 欲しいです form reserved for the speaker's own want.
why: 欲しいです directly states the SPEAKER's own want — it isn't natural for describing someone else's desire.
This means 'doesn't want' — the opposite of the intended meaning.
This states YOUR guess about his want, not the standard way to report his observable behavior.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>は<ruby>注射<rt>ちゅうしゃ</rt></ruby>を＿＿<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>きました。」 (The child cried, scared of the injection)
quiz.ex: がって describes the child's observable fear from outside, leading into 泣きました — 怖がって泣きました, 'cried, showing fear'.
why: 怖い directly states a feeling as if it were the speaker's own — not the outward-behavior pattern needed for describing the child.
This means 'doesn't become scared' — the wrong polarity.
らしい reports hearsay or inference from indirect evidence, not directly observed outward behavior — がって is the more direct match here.

points.fn: About to / in the middle of / just finished
points.explain: ところ pinpoints exactly where you are in an action's timeline. Dictionary form + ところ = right before it starts ('about to'): 今から出かけるところです. ている form + ところ = right in the middle of it ('in the middle of'): 今ご飯を食べているところです. た-form + ところ = the moment right after it finished ('just this instant'): 今ちょうど終わったところです. It's more precise and momentary than たばかり, which allows a looser, more subjective sense of recency.
formation: Verb (dictionary form) + ところ — about to
Verb (ている form) + ところ — in the middle of
Verb (た form) + ところ — just finished, this instant

examples.jp: 今から<ruby>晩<rt>ばん</rt></ruby>ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>るところです。
examples.en: I'm just about to make dinner.

examples.jp: 今、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>をしているところです。
examples.en: We're in the middle of a meeting right now.

examples.jp: ちょうど今、レポートを書き<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったところです。
examples.en: I just this instant finished writing the report.

dialogue.jp: もしもし、今<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>ですか。
dialogue.en: Hello, is now an okay time?

dialogue.jp: すみません、今出かけるところなんです。あとでかけ<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>します。
dialogue.en: Sorry, I'm just about to head out. I'll call you back later.

dialogue.jp: わかりました、じゃあまた後で。
dialogue.en: Got it, talk later then.

points.tip: On the phone, 今〜ところです is the natural way to explain exactly what stage you're at right now — Japanese speakers use it constantly to politely explain why they can or can't talk.

quiz.q: 「今、ちょうどご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を＿＿ところです。」 (I'm right in the middle of eating)
quiz.ex: ている-form + ところ marks being right in the middle of an action.
why: Dictionary form + ところ means 'about to', not mid-action.
た-form + ところ means 'just finished' — the opposite point in the timeline.
The volitional form 食べよう doesn't combine with ところ this way.

quiz.q: Compared to 「今<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたばかりです」, what makes 「今<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたところです」 different?
choices: ところ pinpoints a more precise, momentary instant; ばかり is looser and more subjective about elapsed time
They mean exactly the same thing with no difference
ばかり is more precise than ところ
ところ can only be used for the distant past
quiz.ex: たところ marks a precise, momentary point right after completion, while たばかり expresses a looser sense of 'recently' that can even stretch to things that happened a while ago if they still feel recent.
why: They overlap in meaning but differ in precision, as described above.
It's the reverse — ところ is the more precise, momentary one.
ところ is about a precise point in time, typically close to now, not specifically the distant past.

points.explain: The imperative is the bluntest, most direct way to tell someone to do something — used between close male friends, in sports coaching, on warning signs, and in quoted speech. It's rarely something you need to produce yourself in polite conversation, but recognizing it is essential for reading manga, signs, and quoted dialogue. Godan verbs change their final u-sound to an e-sound (行く→行け, 話す→話せ); ichidan verbs drop る and add ろ (食べる→食べろ, 見る→見ろ); する→しろ and 来る→来い are irregular. Adding な to the plain dictionary form makes a blunt negative command: 行くな ('don't go!').
formation: Godan: final -u → -e (行く→行け, 待つ→待て)
Ichidan: drop る, add ろ (食べる→食べろ, 見る→見ろ)
irregular: する→しろ／来る→来い
negative command: dictionary form + な (行くな)

examples.jp: 「<ruby>危<rt>あぶ</rt></ruby>ない！<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まれ！」
examples.en: "Watch out! Stop!"

examples.jp: 「<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く食べろ！」と父は<ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>って<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いました。
examples.en: "Eat quickly!" my father said angrily.

examples.jp: 「ここに入るな。」という<ruby>看板<rt>かんばん</rt></ruby>がありました。
examples.en: There was a sign that said, "Don't enter here."

dialogue.jp: <ruby>漫画<rt>まんが</rt></ruby>の中で、先生が「もっと<ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>れ！」と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていました。
dialogue.en: In the manga, the teacher said, "Try harder!"

dialogue.jp: <ruby>命令形<rt>めいれいけい</rt></ruby>ですね。<ruby>普段<rt>ふだん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>わない<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>い<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>ですけど、こういう<ruby>場面<rt>ばめん</rt></ruby>ではよく出てきますね。
dialogue.en: That's the imperative form. It's not something you'd normally use yourself, but it shows up a lot in scenes like this.

dialogue.jp: そうですね。読めるようになりたいです。
dialogue.en: Right. I want to be able to read it.

points.tip: You'll meet this form far more often as a READER (manga, signs, quoted speech, movies) than as a speaker — focus on recognizing it instantly rather than producing it, since 〜てください or 〜なさい cover nearly all of your own everyday requests.

quiz.q: 「行く」の<ruby>命令形<rt>めいれいけい</rt></ruby>は？
quiz.ex: Godan verbs shift their final -u sound to -e for the imperative: 行く→行け.
why: 行こう is the volitional ('let's go' / 'I'll go'), not the blunt command form.
行って is the て-form, used for requests like 行ってください — not the bare imperative.
行くな is the NEGATIVE command ('don't go!') — the opposite polarity.

quiz.q: 「食べる」の<ruby>命令形<rt>めいれいけい</rt></ruby>は？
quiz.ex: Ichidan verbs drop る and add ろ for the imperative: 食べる→食べろ.
why: 食べれ isn't a valid ichidan imperative — る is replaced with ろ, not れ.
食べよ is an older, more literary-sounding variant rarely used in everyday modern speech — 食べろ is the standard rough command.
食べて is the て-form, used for polite requests (食べてください), not the blunt imperative.

points.explain: Combine the causative form with てください to politely ask permission to do something yourself — literally 'please make/let me do X'. 使わせてください (please let me use it) is often more natural in daily Japanese than the plain-permission 使ってもいいですか, especially when you want to sound like you're volunteering to take an active role (leading a meeting, trying a task, explaining something), rather than just asking a flat yes/no question.
formation: Verb (causative て-form) + ください
使う → 使わせて＋ください → 使わせてください
休む → 休ませてください

examples.jp: すみません、<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し休ませてください。
examples.en: Excuse me, please let me rest a little.

examples.jp: その<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>にやらせてください。
examples.en: Please let me do that job.

examples.jp: <ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>があるので、ちょっと<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えさせてください。
examples.en: I have a question, so please let me think for a moment.

dialogue.jp: この<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>、だれが<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>しますか。
dialogue.en: Who's going to explain these materials?

dialogue.jp: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>させてください。<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby>してきましたので。
dialogue.en: Please let me explain them — I came prepared.

dialogue.jp: じゃあ、お<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>いします。
dialogue.en: Alright, go ahead then.

points.tip: 〜させてください is a great way to sound proactive and confident in work or study settings — volunteering yourself politely, rather than just asking a flat yes/no question.

quiz.q: 'Please let me try this dish' — pick the best sentence.
choices: この<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>を食べてもいいですか
この<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>を食べさせてください
この<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>を食べさせられます
この<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>を食べてください
quiz.ex: Causative + てください frames it as you politely asking to be allowed to act — 食べさせてください.
why: This asks a plain yes/no permission question — grammatically fine, but a flatter, less proactive framing than the causative-request pattern being tested.
Causative-passive means being MADE to eat — the opposite framing (unwilling), not a request for yourself.
This tells someone ELSE to eat — not a request to act yourself.

quiz.q: 「すみません、今日は<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く＿＿。」 (Excuse me, please let me leave early today)
quiz.ex: Causative + てください politely requests permission for yourself: 帰らせてください.
why: This tells someone ELSE to go home — not a request for yourself.
This is causative-passive, being made to go home unwillingly — the wrong nuance.
This just states your own wish without framing it as a request for permission.

conjugation.label: Group 3 verb
conjugation.to: させてください／来させてください

points.explain: Attach はどうですか to a て-form to gently suggest a course of action — 少し休んではどうですか (How about resting a little?). It's softer and more open-ended than たほうがいいです, which sounds more like firm advice. In casual speech は is often dropped, and たら replaces て entirely: 休んだらどう？／休んだらどうですか is extremely common casually.
formation: Verb (て-form) + はどうですか — polite suggestion
casual variant: Verb (た-form) + らどう？

examples.jp: <ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れているなら、<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し休んではどうですか。
examples.en: If you're tired, how about resting a little?

examples.jp: <ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>、先生に<ruby>相談<rt>そうだん</rt></ruby>してはどうですか。
examples.en: How about consulting your teacher once?

examples.jp: （カジュアル）そんなに<ruby>悩<rt>なや</rt></ruby>んでるなら、聞いてみたらどう？
examples.en: (Casual) If you're worrying that much, how about just asking?

dialogue.jp: <ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby>、あまり<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>れないんです。
dialogue.en: I haven't been sleeping well lately.

dialogue.jp: それなら、<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る前にスマホを見ないようにしてはどうですか。
dialogue.en: In that case, how about trying not to look at your phone before bed?

dialogue.jp: そうですね、<ruby>試<rt>ため</rt></ruby>してみます。
dialogue.en: Good idea, I'll try that.

points.tip: てはどうですか keeps the option gently on the table — pair it with なら ('if that's the case') to sound like natural, caring advice rather than a directive.

quiz.q: Which of these floats the gentlest suggestion?
choices: 休んだほうがいいです
quiz.ex: てはどうですか floats a gentle suggestion — softer than firm advice (ほうがいい), a request (てください), or a direct command (なさい).
why: たほうがいいです reads as firmer, more direct advice.
てください is a direct request.
なさい is a direct command form — the least gentle of the four.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れてるなら、<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し休んだら＿＿？」 (casual suggestion)
quiz.ex: In casual speech, たら + どう (dropping です/か) is a natural, relaxed way to float the same suggestion.
why: どうか sounds like a formal, earnest request phrase, not the casual dropped-です suggestion tone.
どうして means 'why' — unrelated to making a suggestion.
なぜ also means 'why' — unrelated to making a suggestion.

check.q: 「これは＿＿<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>です。」 (the photo I took in Kyoto)
choices: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>で<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>った
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>で<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>った
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>で<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>ります
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>で<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>って
check.ex: Inside a noun-modifying clause the subject takes が, and the verb takes a plain form.

check.q: 「あそこで<ruby>新聞<rt>しんぶん</rt></ruby>を読んでいる人は父です。」— what does 読んでいる modify?
check.ex: The clause sits directly in front of 人 and describes which person is meant.

check.q: 「<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が来る＿＿、まだ<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません。」
check.ex: かどうか embeds a yes/no question inside a bigger sentence.

check.q: 「この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>有名<rt>ゆうめい</rt></ruby>＿＿、聞いてみましょう。」 (na-adjective + whether or not)
check.ex: だ is dropped directly before かどうか: 有名かどうか.

check.q: 「日本に来た＿＿なので、まだ<ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>がいません。」
check.ex: 〜たばかり means you only just did something, which explains not having friends yet.

check.q: 「<ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>を＿＿。」 (she wants one — you can tell)
check.ex: がる describes another person's want as something you observe from the outside.

check.q: 「<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>はいつも外で＿＿。」 (he always wants to play outside)
check.ex: 〜たい drops い and takes がる for a third person: 遊びたがる.

check.q: 「今、ちょうど<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>を出る＿＿です。」 (about to leave)
check.ex: Dictionary form + ところ marks the moment right before an action starts.

check.q: 「ちょうど今、<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった＿＿です。」 (this very instant)
check.ex: た-form + ところ pinpoints the moment just after finishing — more precise than ばかり.

check.q: 「<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ」の<ruby>命令形<rt>めいれいけい</rt></ruby>は？
check.ex: Godan verbs shift the final -u to -e: 待つ → 待て.

check.q: 「見る」の<ruby>命令形<rt>めいれいけい</rt></ruby>は？
check.ex: Ichidan verbs drop る and add ろ: 見る → 見ろ.

check.q: 「ここに入る＿＿。」 (a blunt 'don't enter', as on a sign)
check.ex: Dictionary form + な is the blunt negative command.

check.q: 「その<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に＿＿。」 (please let me do it)
check.ex: Causative + てください politely asks to be allowed to do something yourself.

check.q: 「<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れているなら、<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し休ん＿＿。」 (a gentle suggestion)
check.ex: 〜てはどうですか floats a suggestion more softly than a request or firm advice.

reading: けいご（そんけいご・けんじょうご）

points.explain: <ruby>尊敬語<rt>そんけいご</rt></ruby> lifts up the person you're talking about — a customer, a teacher, a superior, someone else's family. You never use it about yourself. Three shapes cover almost everything at N4: the regular お＋stem＋になる pattern, the passive-shaped 〜れる／られる (the lightest, most everyday honorific), and a short list of irregular verbs that replace the word entirely. Recognizing these matters long before you can produce them — every station announcement and shop greeting in Japan is built from them.
formation: お＋Verb(ます-stem)＋になる — <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ → お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちになる
ご＋する-noun＋になる — <ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>する → ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>になる
Verb passive form 〜れる／られる — <ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>られる（lightest honorific）
irregular: 行く・来る・いる → いらっしゃる ／ 食べる・飲む → <ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し上がる ／ 見る → ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になる ／ <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う → おっしゃる ／ する → なさる

examples.jp: <ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はもうお<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りになりました。
examples.en: The company president has already gone home.

examples.jp: 先生は何時に来られますか。
examples.en: What time is the teacher coming? (light honorific)

examples.jp: こちらのパンフレットをご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になりましたか。
examples.en: Have you looked at this pamphlet?

examples.jp: <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は今、<ruby>会議室<rt>かいぎしつ</rt></ruby>にいらっしゃいます。
examples.en: The manager is in the meeting room right now.

dialogue.jp: <ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby><ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>はもういらっしゃいましたか。
dialogue.en: Has manager Yamada arrived yet?

dialogue.jp: はい、先ほどお<ruby>着<rt>き</rt></ruby>きになりました。
dialogue.en: Yes, he arrived a little while ago.

dialogue.jp: では、ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>します。
dialogue.en: Then I'll show you through.

points.tip: 〜れる／られる looks exactly like the passive, so context decides which one you're reading. If the subject is someone you'd be polite to, it's almost certainly honorific, not passive.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はもう＿＿。」 (honorific — the president went home)
choices: お<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りになりました
quiz.ex: お＋stem＋になる raises the president's action. お<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りする would be humble, which wrongly lowers him.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>会議室<rt>かいぎしつ</rt></ruby>に＿＿。」 (honorific for いる)
quiz.ex: いらっしゃる is the honorific for いる／行く／来る. おる is the humble form, used about yourself.

quiz.q: 「先生がそう＿＿。」 (honorific for <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う)
quiz.ex: おっしゃる is honorific 'to say'. <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>す is the humble version for your own speech.

points.explain: <ruby>謙譲語<rt>けんじょうご</rt></ruby> works from the opposite direction: instead of raising the other person, you lower yourself, which has the same net effect of showing respect. Use it for your own actions — and for your own group's actions when speaking to an outsider, which is why staff say <ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります ('our person will come') rather than raising their own colleague. The regular pattern is お＋stem＋する, plus a short irregular list.
formation: お＋Verb(ます-stem)＋する — <ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>つ → お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちする
ご＋する-noun＋する — <ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>する → ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>する

irregular: 行く・来る → <ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る ／ いる → おる ／ <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う → <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>す ／ 見る → <ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>する ／ 聞く・<ruby>訪<rt>たず</rt></ruby>ねる → うかがう ／ する → いたす ／ もらう → いただく

examples.jp: お<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>をお<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちします。
examples.en: I'll carry your luggage.

examples.jp: <ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>がすぐに<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります。
examples.en: The person in charge will come right away.

examples.jp: 先生の<ruby>作品<rt>さくひん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>しました。
examples.en: I looked at the teacher's work.

examples.jp: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、先生のお<ruby>宅<rt>たく</rt></ruby>にうかがいます。
examples.en: I'll visit the teacher's home tomorrow.

dialogue.jp: この<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>、だれが<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>しますか。
dialogue.en: Who will explain these materials?

dialogue.jp: わたくしがご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>いたします。
dialogue.en: I will explain them.

dialogue.jp: では、お<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>いします。
dialogue.en: Please go ahead, then.

points.tip: The classic mistake is using お〜する about someone else — お待ちしてください is wrong. Requests to the other person take お待ちください (honorific); お待ちします is only ever about yourself.

quiz.q: 「わたしが<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>を＿＿。」 (humble — I'll bring it)
quiz.ex: お＋stem＋する lowers your own action. お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちになる would raise it, which you never do about yourself.

quiz.q: 「先生の<ruby>絵<rt>え</rt></ruby>を＿＿。」 (humble — I looked at it)
choices: ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になりました
quiz.ex: <ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>する is the humble verb for viewing something belonging to a superior. ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になる is honorific.

quiz.q: 「<ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>がすぐに＿＿。」 (humble — our staff will come)
quiz.ex: Speaking to an outsider about your own side, even a colleague takes the humble <ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る, not an honorific.

points.jp: <ruby>接客<rt>せっきゃく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>を聞き<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>る
points.fn: Understanding the keigo staff use on you
points.explain: As a visitor you are almost never required to produce keigo — です／ます is completely acceptable and expected. What you do need is to understand it instantly, because shop, station and hotel staff use it at speed. These set phrases are worth knowing as whole units rather than parsing them grammatically in the moment: you'll hear the same dozen lines everywhere you go.
formation: いらっしゃいませ — welcome (said to you on entering)
かしこまりました／<ruby>承知<rt>しょうち</rt></ruby>しました — certainly, understood
<ruby>少々<rt>しょうしょう</rt></ruby>お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください — please wait a moment
お<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>まりでしょうか — have you decided?
<ruby>恐<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>れ入りますが〜 — I'm sorry to trouble you, but...

examples.jp: いらっしゃいませ。<ruby>何名様<rt>なんめいさま</rt></ruby>でいらっしゃいますか。
examples.en: Welcome. How many in your party?

examples.jp: <ruby>恐<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>れ入りますが、こちらにお名前をお書きください。
examples.en: Sorry to trouble you, but please write your name here.

examples.jp: ただいま<ruby>係<rt>かかり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>りますので、<ruby>少々<rt>しょうしょう</rt></ruby>お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください。
examples.en: Someone will be with you shortly, so please wait a moment.

examples.jp: こちらのお<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>にどうぞ。
examples.en: Please take this seat.

dialogue.jp: いらっしゃいませ。ご<ruby>注文<rt>ちゅうもん</rt></ruby>はお<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>まりでしょうか。
dialogue.en: Welcome. Have you decided on your order?

dialogue.jp: すみません、もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってください。
dialogue.en: Sorry, could you give me a moment?

dialogue.jp: かしこまりました。お<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>まりになりましたらお<ruby>呼<rt>よ</rt></ruby>びください。
dialogue.en: Certainly. Please call me when you've decided.

points.tip: Answering keigo with plain です／ます is completely natural and not rude — staff do not expect keigo back from a customer. Trying to force it usually sounds stranger than just being clear and polite.

quiz.q: Staff say 「<ruby>少々<rt>しょうしょう</rt></ruby>お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください。」 You should:
quiz.ex: <ruby>少々<rt>しょうしょう</rt></ruby>お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください is the keigo form of ちょっと<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってください.

quiz.q: 「お<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>まりでしょうか。」 is asking:
quiz.ex: <ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>まる ('to be decided') in honorific form — staff asking if you're ready to order.

check.q: 「<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はもう＿＿。」 (honorific)
choices: お<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りになりました
check.ex: お＋stem＋になる raises the other person's action.

check.q: 「わたしが<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を＿＿。」 (humble)
check.ex: お＋stem＋する lowers your own action.

check.q: 「先生は何時に＿＿か。」 (honorific for 来る)
check.ex: いらっしゃる covers 行く・来る・いる in honorific speech.

check.q: 「<ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>がすぐに＿＿。」 (your own side, to an outsider)
check.ex: Your own group takes humble forms when you speak to someone outside it.

check.q: 「先生がそう＿＿。」 (honorific for <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う)
check.ex: おっしゃる is honorific; <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>す is humble.

check.q: 「わたくしは<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>と＿＿。」 (humble self-introduction)
check.ex: <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>す is the humble verb for saying your own name.

check.q: 「どうぞ＿＿ください。」 (honorific for 食べる)
check.ex: <ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し上がる is honorific 'to eat'; いただく is humble, for your own eating.

check.q: 「先生の<ruby>絵<rt>え</rt></ruby>を＿＿。」 (humble)
choices: ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になりました
check.ex: <ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>する is humble viewing; ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になる is honorific.

check.q: 「<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、先生のお<ruby>宅<rt>たく</rt></ruby>に＿＿。」 (humble visiting)
check.ex: うかがう is the humble verb for visiting a superior.

check.q: Which is WRONG when asking the other person to wait?
choices: <ruby>少々<rt>しょうしょう</rt></ruby>お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください
お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちいただけますか
check.ex: お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちします is humble — it describes YOUR waiting, so it can't be a request aimed at someone else.

check.q: 「ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>＿＿。」 (honorific: do you use it?)
check.ex: ご＋noun＋になる is the honorific pattern for する-nouns.

check.q: 「かしこまりました」 is said by:
check.ex: It's humble service language meaning 'certainly' — you hear it far more than you say it.

check.q: 「<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>会議室<rt>かいぎしつ</rt></ruby>に＿＿。」 (honorific for いる)
check.ex: いらっしゃる for someone else; おる is the humble equivalent for yourself.

check.q: As a visitor in Japan, answering staff keigo with plain です／ます is:
check.ex: Customers aren't expected to return keigo — clear, polite です／ます is entirely normal.
